extracted.intended_audience: journalism researchers, newsroom editors, and media analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical criteria about which stories are placed in lead/front-page positions in U.S. newspapers, focusing on how story framing (competitive vs. explanatory) affects prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive/Conflict framing increases lead placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories emphasizing conflict, winning/losing, and wrongdoing comprise 35% of lead stories despite representing only 31% of all stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use or identify competitive frames (conflict, contest, wrongdoing) when the goal is prominent placement; empirical implication is that such frames are disproportionately selected for lead positions because they convey higher perceived news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory/historical/process/trend frames receive lower placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories using historical, process, and trend frames appear in lead position just 8% of the time, though they are 13% of all stories, and they occupy 17% of lower-page positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanatory framing tends to be de-prioritized for top placement; if aiming for front-page prominence, avoid packaging a piece primarily as background, process, or trend without a competitive element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame matters as much as topic for placement decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The research asserts that 'story frame matters as much as topic' — how a story is framed (e.g., competitive vs. explanatory) is as influential as the subject matter in determining front-page placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating stories for prominence, assess framing explicitly (not just topic); a story on the same topic can have very different placement outcomes depending on frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors select based on perceived importance
rubrics_metrics.description: One proposed explanation is importance-based selection — editors view competitive framing as signaling greater urgency or importance and thus select those stories for prominent placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To align with editorial selection, present elements that signal urgency or importance (timeliness, stakes, conflict) when pitching or editing stories for front placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors select based on perceived audience appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative proposed explanation is audience appeal — a competitively framed story is thought to be more likely to appeal to readers and therefore should be near the top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame copy and lede to maximize anticipated reader interest; frames that emphasize contest or wrongdoing may be preferred because editors believe they attract readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing shapes conveyed news value
rubrics_metrics.description: Key conclusion: 'Stories framed around competitiveness ... are placed in such a way as to convey greater news value.' Framing itself is used to communicate a story's newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider framing as a tool to communicate news value to both editors and readers; editorial placement decisions can be influenced by how much news value the frame implies.
